passage.bullet: Twelve Tables → Ancient Roman code establishing clear written laws.
basilica → Grand stone town hall where Roman court cases were heard.
magistrate → Senior Roman judge who weighed witness evidence and set fines.

context.bullet: After AD 43, Rome introduced Britain’s first written laws rooted in the Twelve Tables, judged by town magistrates inside stone basilicas.
Yet Roman towns still had no police detectives to hunt down everyday thieves.

passage.bullet: vigiles → Night-watchmen who watched streets for fires rather than solving thefts.
Roman citizens → Privileged people who usually paid fines or faced exile.
enslaved people → Workers with no rights who faced whipping, mines, or the arena.

context.bullet: Victims had to catch suspects themselves, and courts fined wealthy citizens while whipping or condemning enslaved people.
When nobody saw a thief strike, victims could not bring anyone to court.

passage.bullet: Aquae Sulis → Roman spa town at Bath built around steaming sacred springs.
curse tablets → Thin folded lead sheets scratched with Latin pleas against thieves.
Sulis Minerva → Goddess asked to punish unseen bathhouse cloak thieves.

context.bullet: At Aquae Sulis Bath, angry bathers scratched Latin pleas onto folded lead curse tablets asking goddess Sulis Minerva to punish cloak thieves.
When Roman rule ended in AD 410, Anglo-Saxon villages built community justice instead.

passage.bullet: tithing → Group of ten neighbours aged twelve and over answering for one another.
King’s Peace → Lawful village order that every tithing promised to protect.
Hue and Cry → Loud horn and shout alarm forcing every villager to chase a thief.

context.bullet: Every male villager aged twelve joined a ten-person tithing and had to chase thieves immediately whenever the Hue and Cry horn sounded.
Once neighbours caught a wrongdoer, villages needed a peaceful way to settle anger.

passage.bullet: blood feud → Deadly cycle of revenge attacks between two angry families.
wergild → Fixed silver "person-price" paid to an injured victim’s family.
King Alfred the Great → Ruler who gathered English laws into his written Domboc law code.

context.bullet: Royal law codes fixed silver wergild "person-price" payments to stop family blood feuds, though noble thanes were valued six times above ceorl farmers.
When no witnesses saw a crime and oaths clashed, courts turned to the Church.

passage.bullet: Hundred Court → Monthly open-air local court where elders heard witness oaths.
Trial by Ordeal → Last-resort church test asking God to reveal guilt or innocence.
Trial by Hot Iron → Carrying glowing iron three paces before checking the bandaged hand three days later.

context.bullet: When oath-helpers at the Hundred Court could not settle a dispute, priests held Trial by Hot Iron or Cold Water trusting God to judge.
In 1066, Norman Conquest brought royal Forest Laws and travelling judges.

passage.bullet: William the Conqueror → Norman king who kept tithings yet created royal hunting reserves.
Forest Laws → Strict Norman rules banning villagers from hunting deer or cutting wood.
poaching → Secretly hunting deer or rabbits on royal or lordly land.

context.bullet: William I kept Saxon tithings and the Hue and Cry, shifted fines to the King’s treasury, and banned peasant deer hunting under harsh Forest Laws.
A century later, Henry II unified patchwork courts under royal judges.

passage.bullet: Common Law → One shared English legal system enforced by Henry II’s travelling judges.
jury → Twelve sworn neighbours weighing courtroom evidence to decide verdicts.
Magna Carta → 1215 charter sealed by King John promising lawful trials.

context.bullet: Henry II’s travelling judges built one Common Law with twelve-person juries, cemented in 1215 by Magna Carta and the Pope’s ban on Ordeals.
Alongside royal courts, cathedrals and market squares shaped everyday medieval justice.

passage.bullet: Durham Cathedral → Northern cathedral famous for its twelfth-century bronze lion Sanctuary Knocker.
sanctuary → Safe Church shelter lasting up to forty days before trial or exile.
pillory → Upright wooden frame locking a dishonest trader’s head and wrists.

context.bullet: Fugitives striking cathedral knockers claimed up to forty days of Church sanctuary, while market towns shamed cheats in wooden stocks and pillories.
By 1500, Tudor monarchs began curbing sanctuary as poverty and treason fears rose.

passage.bullet: vagrants → Homeless jobless people wandering from parish to parish.
1601 Poor Law → Elizabethan Act aiding elderly locals while punishing able-bodied beggars.
sturdy beggars → Tudor label for healthy jobless people whipped behind carts.

context.bullet: Rising poverty put vagrants on Tudor roads; the 1601 Poor Law aided sick locals while whipping healthy "sturdy beggars" behind carts.
Alongside fear of vagrants, religious division sparked deadly treason plots.

passage.bullet: High Treason → Plotting to kill the monarch or destroy Parliament.
Monteagle Letter → Unsigned warning note that tipped off King James I before 5 November 1605.
dark lantern → Shuttered iron candle holder seized with Guy Fawkes beside 36 barrels.

context.bullet: Alerted by the Monteagle Letter on 4–5 November 1605, guards caught Guy Fawkes beside 36 gunpowder barrels and punished High Treason fiercely.

passage.bullet: superstition → Blaming bad harvests or illness on magic instead of natural causes.
Matthew Hopkins → East Anglian "Witchfinder General" who charged towns fees in 1645–1647.
Royal Society → Scientific group founded in 1660 encouraging rational proof over magic.

context.bullet: Civil War panic let Matthew Hopkins accuse East Anglian women in 1645–1647, until post-1660 peace, science, and strict judges ended witch trials.
By 1700, witch trials faded—yet Georgian MPs soon created the "Bloody Code".

passage.bullet: import taxes → Heavy customs duties making legal tea, silk, and brandy expensive.
smuggling → Secretly landing untaxed barrels onto dark coves at night.
highwaymen → Mounted pistol robbers like Dick Turpin holding up lonely coaches.

context.bullet: Heavy tea taxes fuelled midnight coastal smuggling, while unlit roads and flintlock pistols let highwaymen rob cash-carrying stagecoaches.
Frightened landowners in Parliament answered with over 220 death-penalty laws.

twelve-person juries → Ordinary jurors who undervalued stolen goods to spare petty thieves.

context.bullet: Refusing to fund police, MPs passed over 220 death-penalty laws "the Bloody Code", yet sympathetic juries refused to hang petty thieves.

Sir Alec Jeffreys → Leicester University scientist who discovered genetic DNA profiling in 1984.
DNA profiling → Forensic test identifying guilty offenders and clearing innocent suspects.

context.bullet: Scotland Yard’s 1901 Fingerprint Bureau, 1937 999 calls, and Sir Alec Jeffreys’s 1984 Leicester DNA profiling replaced guesswork with scientific forensics.
